questions.stem: Earth's early atmosphere was derived mainly from:
options: oxygen released by forests that covered the continents at that time
gases captured from the solar wind after the oceans had already formed
evaporation of the oceans, which released oxygen and hydrogen gas
volcanic outgassing during the cooling and differentiation of Earth
questions.explanation: As the young Earth cooled and differentiated, gases escaped from its interior through volcanic activity. Land plants did not appear until billions of years later.

questions.stem: Which gases made up most of the early atmosphere produced by volcanic outgassing?
options: Oxygen and ozone, with only small amounts of water vapour and nitrogen
Hydrogen and helium only, the same gases that make up the Sun itself
Water vapour, carbon dioxide and nitrogen, with almost no free oxygen
Oxygen, nitrogen and argon, in much the same proportions as today
questions.explanation: Volcanoes release mainly water vapour and carbon dioxide, with nitrogen and sulfur gases. Free oxygen was almost absent until photosynthesising organisms produced it.

questions.stem: Nitrogen was a small part of the gas released by early volcanoes, yet it now makes up about 78% of the atmosphere. Why?
options: Nitrogen is produced in large amounts by photosynthesis in the oceans each year
Nitrogen was delivered by comets long after all the other gases had escaped
Nitrogen is heavier than every other gas, so it alone was held by Earth's gravity as others escaped
Nitrogen is unreactive, so it built up while water vapour and carbon dioxide were removed
questions.explanation: Water vapour condensed into the oceans and carbon dioxide was dissolved and locked into rocks, but nitrogen was not removed on a similar scale. It accumulated over billions of years to dominate the air.

questions.stem: The early atmosphere contained far more carbon dioxide than today. Where did most of this carbon dioxide go?
options: It escaped into space because carbon dioxide is lighter than all of the other atmospheric gases
It was converted into nitrogen by lightning strikes in the early atmosphere
It sank into the core, where it reacted with iron to form the inner core
It dissolved in the oceans and was locked into carbonate rocks and buried organic matter
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater and was precipitated as carbonate minerals such as limestone. Photosynthesis also converted it to organic carbon, some of which was buried in sediments.

questions.stem: Which organisms first added significant amounts of oxygen to the atmosphere?
options: Flowering plants growing on the early continents
Fish and other animals living in the early oceans
Fungi that decomposed dead material in the soil
Photosynthesising cyanobacteria in shallow seas
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria, which built stromatolites, were the first organisms to carry out photosynthesis that releases oxygen. Plants and animals appeared much later.

questions.stem: Which word equation summarises photosynthesis, the process that changed the composition of the atmosphere?
options: Water → hydrogen + oxygen, using heat from volcanic activity
Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, releasing energy
Nitrogen + oxygen → nitrogen oxides, using lightning energy
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen. The reverse reaction is respiration.

questions.stem: Oxygen produced by early cyanobacteria did not build up in the atmosphere straight away. Why not?
options: It was converted into nitrogen by bacteria living in the sediment of the sea floor
It reacted with iron dissolved in seawater, forming iron oxides that settled on the sea floor
It was all used by animals for respiration as soon as it entered the shallow coastal seas of the time
It escaped into space because oxygen is lighter than every other atmospheric gas
questions.explanation: Early oceans held large amounts of dissolved iron. Oxygen reacted with it to form insoluble iron oxides, which settled out as the iron-rich bands of banded iron formations. Animals had not yet evolved.

questions.stem: What are banded iron formations?
options: Metamorphic rocks of alternating mica and quartz bands formed deep in mountain belts
Soil layers of alternating iron and clay formed by weathering of rock on dry land
Sedimentary rocks of alternating iron oxide and silica-rich layers deposited in ancient seas
Igneous rocks of alternating basalt and granite layers formed by repeated lava eruptions
questions.explanation: Banded iron formations are chemical sedimentary rocks with layers of iron oxides, such as hematite and magnetite, alternating with chert. Western Australia's Pilbara contains very large examples.

questions.stem: Most banded iron formations were deposited before about 1.8 billion years ago. Which interpretation is consistent with this?
options: Once most dissolved iron was removed from seawater, oxygen could build up in the oceans and air
Oxygen production stopped 1.8 billion years ago, so no more iron oxide could form after that
The oceans dried up 1.8 billion years ago, so no further sediment of any kind was deposited
Iron stopped reaching the Earth's surface 1.8 billion years ago because the core had frozen
questions.explanation: While dissolved iron was abundant, it consumed the oxygen produced. When that iron sink was largely used up, oxygen could accumulate. Photosynthesis continued, so oxygen production did not stop.

questions.stem: Rounded grains of pyrite, an iron sulfide that breaks down quickly in oxygen-rich air, are found in river sediments older than about 2.4 billion years but not in younger ones. What does this suggest?
options: Rivers did not exist before about 2.4 billion years ago, so pyrite grains could not form
Pyrite formed only after 2.4 billion years ago, when oxygen first reached the oceans
The atmosphere contained very little oxygen before about 2.4 billion years ago
The atmosphere contained more oxygen before 2.4 billion years ago than it does today
questions.explanation: Pyrite grains could only survive being weathered and carried by rivers if there was little oxygen to break them down. Their disappearance in younger sediments is evidence the atmosphere became oxygenated.

questions.stem: As oxygen built up in the atmosphere, an ozone layer formed in the stratosphere. Why was this important for life?
options: Ozone absorbed carbon dioxide from the air, preventing the planet from overheating
Ozone absorbed much of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation, allowing life to colonise the land
Ozone supplied oxygen for respiration directly to the organisms living in the deep oceans below
Ozone trapped heat near the surface, warming the planet enough for oceans to form
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet radiation damages DNA. Once the ozone layer filtered much of it, organisms could survive on land and in shallow water exposed to sunlight.

questions.stem: Understanding the oxygenation of the atmosphere required knowledge from several disciplines. Which pair of evidence from different disciplines best supports this event?
options: Seismic shadow zones from geophysics and the meteorite compositions that are studied in astronomy
Historical weather diaries from history and modern satellite images used in meteorology
Fossil stromatolites from palaeontology and the iron oxide chemistry of banded iron formations
Ice core air bubbles from glaciology and the tree-ring records studied in botany
questions.explanation: Fossils show oxygen-producing microbes existed, while the chemistry of iron oxides and other minerals shows when oxygen reacted and accumulated. Integrating chemistry and palaeontology improved understanding of the event.

questions.stem: Which list best gives the approximate composition of the modern dry atmosphere?
options: Nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, argon about 1%, carbon dioxide about 0.04%
Oxygen 78%, nitrogen 21%, argon about 1%, carbon dioxide about 0.04%
Nitrogen 50%, oxygen 30%, carbon dioxide 15%, argon about 5%
Carbon dioxide 78%, nitrogen 21%, oxygen about 1%, argon about 0.04%
questions.explanation: Today's air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, very different from the carbon dioxide-rich, oxygen-poor early atmosphere. Living organisms account for most of the change.

questions.stem: Which list gives the layers of the atmosphere in order upwards from Earth's surface?
options: Stratosphere, troposphere, thermosphere, mesosphere
Troposphere, mesosphere, stratosphere, thermosphere
Thermosphere, mesosphere, stratosphere, troposphere
Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere
questions.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest layer, then the stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere. Each boundary, such as the tropopause, marks a change in the temperature trend.

questions.stem: The atmosphere is divided into layers on the basis of:
options: the height at which aircraft and satellites can travel
the amount of nitrogen compared with oxygen in each
changes in the way temperature varies with altitude
changes in the colour of the sky seen from the ground
questions.explanation: Temperature decreases with height in some layers and increases in others. The boundaries are placed where the trend reverses.

questions.stem: Which feature describes the troposphere?
options: It is the coldest layer, where meteors burn up high above the ozone layer
It is the highest layer, where the air is extremely thin and absorbs X-rays
Temperature falls with height, and it contains nearly all weather and most of the air's mass
Temperature rises with height, because the ozone it contains absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun
questions.explanation: The troposphere is heated mainly from below by Earth's surface, so it is warmest at the bottom. Rising and sinking air in it produces clouds and weather.

questions.stem: Why does temperature increase with height in the stratosphere?
options: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun
The stratosphere is closer to the Sun, so it receives much more heat
Heat rising from Earth's surface collects at the top of the stratosphere
Clouds in the stratosphere trap infrared radiation from the ground
questions.explanation: Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and converts the energy to heat. Absorption is strongest in the upper stratosphere, so temperatures rise with height up to about 50 km.

questions.stem: In which layer does temperature decrease with height to the coldest point in the atmosphere, and where most meteors burn up?
options: The stratosphere
The thermosphere
The mesosphere
The troposphere
questions.explanation: Above the stratopause, there is little ozone to absorb sunlight, so temperature falls with height through the mesosphere to below about −80 °C. Meteors heat and burn up as they hit its gas molecules.

questions.stem: Temperatures in the thermosphere can exceed 1000 °C, yet a person there would not feel hot. Why?
options: Heat cannot travel at all through the thermosphere because it is a vacuum
The air is so thin that very few molecules transfer heat, though each moves fast
The thermosphere contains only ozone, which cannot transfer heat to any object
The temperature is measured only at night, when the thermosphere is coldest
questions.explanation: Temperature measures the average energy of the molecules. Thermosphere molecules absorb high-energy solar radiation and move very fast, but there are so few of them that little heat is transferred.

questions.stem: A weather balloon records 15 °C at the surface, falling steadily to −55 °C at 11 km. Above that the temperature stays nearly constant, then rises to about 0 °C at 50 km. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The stratopause is near 11 km, and the balloon then rose through the mesosphere
The mesopause is near 11 km, and the balloon then rose through the thermosphere
The balloon stayed in the troposphere, since temperature rose above 11 km
The tropopause is near 11 km, and the balloon then rose through the stratosphere
questions.explanation: Falling temperature marks the troposphere, and the change in trend at about 11 km is the tropopause. Rising temperature from ozone heating identifies the stratosphere, which ends near 50 km.

questions.stem: Air temperature in the troposphere falls by about 6.5 °C per kilometre of height. If it is 20 °C at sea level, what is the temperature 4 km above?
questions.explanation: Fall in temperature = 6.5 × 4 = 26 °C, so 20 − 26 = −6 °C. Subtracting 26 from zero, or adding it, gives the other values.

questions.stem: Water is present on the surface of Earth mainly as a result of:
options: volcanic outgassing and impacts by icy bodies from space
photosynthesis and respiration by early microorganisms
nuclear reactions in Earth's core that produce new water
lightning strikes that combine nitrogen and oxygen gases
questions.explanation: Water vapour released by volcanoes condensed as Earth cooled, and impacts of comets and water-rich asteroids added more water to the young planet.

questions.stem: The ratio of deuterium (heavy hydrogen) to ordinary hydrogen in Earth's oceans is closer to that measured in some water-rich asteroid meteorites than to that measured in most comets studied so far. What does this suggest?
options: Asteroid-like bodies, along with outgassing, may have supplied more of Earth's water than comets
Comets supplied all of Earth's water, because their deuterium ratio differs from that of the oceans
None of Earth's water came from space, because no ratio matches the oceans exactly
Earth's water formed recently from hydrogen in the solar wind reacting with rock
questions.explanation: Matching isotope ratios suggest a common source. The evidence favours water-rich asteroids over most comets measured, though scientists continue to test this as more bodies are studied.

questions.stem: Why can water exist on Earth's surface as a solid, a liquid and a gas at the same time?
options: Earth's gravity converts liquid water into ice and vapour continually
Water molecules change chemically into different substances in each phase
Surface temperatures and pressures span the conditions for all three phases
Water's boiling point is below its freezing point on Earth's surface
questions.explanation: Earth's surface temperatures range from well below to above 0 °C, so ice sheets, oceans and water vapour coexist. Changes of phase move energy as well as water through Earth systems.

questions.stem: How did the first oceans form on the early Earth?
options: Photosynthesising organisms produced water as a waste product over millions of years
Water vapour in the atmosphere condensed and fell as rain once the surface had cooled
Ice from the core melted and seeped upward through cracks in the newly formed crust
Hydrogen and oxygen from the Sun combined in the oceans' basins during solar flares
questions.explanation: When the surface cooled below the boiling point of water, outgassed water vapour condensed and rained out, filling low-lying basins. Zircon evidence suggests liquid water existed very early in Earth's history.

questions.stem: Which process in the water cycle releases water vapour from plant leaves into the atmosphere?
options: Condensation
Precipitation
Transpiration
Infiltration
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour through the stomata of leaves. Together with evaporation it is often called evapotranspiration.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the energy that drives the water cycle?
options: Earth's internal heat drives all parts of the water cycle, including rainfall
Wind energy alone drives the water cycle, without any energy from the Sun
Solar energy drives evaporation, and gravity drives precipitation and runoff
Gravity drives evaporation, and solar energy drives precipitation and runoff
questions.explanation: Energy from the Sun evaporates water, which is stored as latent heat in the vapour. Gravity then brings water back down as precipitation and moves it downhill as runoff and groundwater flow.

questions.stem: Which list places Earth's water reservoirs in order from largest to smallest volume?
options: The atmosphere, oceans, groundwater, ice sheets and glaciers
Oceans, ice sheets and glaciers, groundwater, the atmosphere
Groundwater, oceans, the atmosphere, ice sheets and glaciers
Ice sheets and glaciers, oceans, the atmosphere, groundwater
questions.explanation: Oceans hold about 97% of Earth's water. Ice sheets and glaciers hold most of the fresh water, followed by groundwater. The atmosphere holds only a tiny fraction at any time.

questions.stem: In which reservoir does a water molecule typically stay for the shortest time?
options: Deep groundwater, about a few days
The atmosphere, about nine days
The deep ocean, about a few weeks
The Antarctic ice sheet, about one year
questions.explanation: Water vapour typically condenses and falls as precipitation within about nine days. Deep ocean water and ice sheets can hold water for thousands of years, and deep groundwater for even longer.

questions.stem: During the last glacial maximum, global sea level was about 120 m lower than today. Which explanation links the water cycle to this change?
options: Ocean water froze into floating sea ice, which took up less volume than liquid water
Ocean water seeped down into the mantle through cracks opened by the cold
Rainfall increased over the oceans, so seawater was carried away to space
Water evaporated from the oceans fell as snow and was stored in ice sheets on land
questions.explanation: When ice sheets grow, water leaves the ocean and is held on land for thousands of years, lowering sea level. Floating sea ice displaces its own weight of water, so freezing it does not lower sea level.

questions.stem: During a long dry summer, a river keeps flowing even though no rain has fallen for months. Where does its water come from?
options: Water created by chemical reactions between rocks in the river bed
Groundwater discharging into the river channel from surrounding aquifers
Water vapour condensing directly onto the river surface from the air
Seawater flowing upstream from the river mouth all the way to the source
questions.explanation: Rain that infiltrated earlier recharges aquifers, and groundwater slowly seeps into rivers, providing baseflow. This links the groundwater and surface parts of the water cycle.
